items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
[MATH: x − 2y = − 5; − 3x + 6y = 15]

Content:
To solve the system, we can reduce [MATH: M] to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

Content:
[MATH: M|∼[1|− 2|− 5; − 3|6|15]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + 3R_{1}; ∼[1|− 2|− 5; 0|0|0].]

Content:
The corresponding system is now
[MATH: x − 2y = − 5; 0x + 0y = 0.]

Content:
Since any pair of numbers [MATH: x,y] is a solution of the final equation [MATH: 0x+0y = 0,] we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

Content:
[MATH: x - 2y = -5.]

Content:
Finally, we describe the general solution of our system.

Content:
- The first variable in our equation, [MATH: x,] is called a basic variable.
- The second variable in our equation, [MATH: y,] is called a free variable.

Content:
Solving for the basic variable [MATH: (x)] in terms of the free variable [MATH: (y),] we get [MATH: x = -5+2y.] So the general solution of the system is
[MATH: x = − 5 + 2y; y = y]
where the free variable [MATH: y] is any number.

Content:
In vector form, this solution is written as
[MATH: [x; y] = [− 5 + 2y; y] = [− 5; 0] + y[2; 1], y ∈ (− ∞, ∞).]

Content:
Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

Content:
If we want to find some particular solution of the system, we simply choose some particular value of [MATH: y] and find the corresponding value of [MATH: x] on the line. For example, if we choose [MATH: y=0,] then the corresponding value is [MATH: x=-5] and the particular solution is [MATH: x=-5,] [MATH: y=0.]

where [MATH: y] is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

[MATH: [x; y] = [1 + 3y; y] = ⟨1 + 3y, y⟩, y ∈ (− ∞, ∞).]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

[MATH: 2|5|4; 4|10|0]

Reducing [MATH: M] to row echelon form, we have [MATH: M|∼[2|5|4; 4|10|0]|R_{1}|:=(1)/(2)R_{1}; ∼[1|(5)/(2)|2; 4|10|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 4)R_{1}; ∼[1|(5)/(2)|2; 0|0|− 8].]

The corresponding system is now [MATH: x + (5)/(2)y = 2; 0x + 0y = − 8.]

However, the final equation [MATH: 0x+0y=-8] has no solution. It simplifies to [MATH: 0=-8,] which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair [MATH: x,y] that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

items.title: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System

sections.normalized_html: Given a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:
sections.readable_text: Given a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

sections.normalized_html:
• The system has exactly one solution if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called consistent independent.

  • The system has infinitely many solutions if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only [MATH: 0]'s. These systems are called consistent dependent.

  • The system has no solution if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only [MATH: 0]'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called inconsistent systems.

The corresponding system is now

[MATH: x − 3y = 1; 0x + 0y = 0.]

Since any pair of numbers [MATH: x,y] is a solution of the final equation [MATH: 0x+0y = 0,] we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

[MATH: x - 3y = 1.]

The first variable [MATH: (x)] is the basic variable, and the second variable [MATH: (y)] is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable [MATH: (x)] in terms of the free variable [MATH: (y),] we get [MATH: x=1+3y,] and the general solution is

[MATH: x = 1 + 3y; y = y]

where [MATH: y] is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

[MATH: [x; y] = [1 + 3y; y] = ⟨1 + 3y, y⟩, y ∈ (− ∞, ∞).]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Singular Systems with No Solution

Content:
Sometimes, a system of equations might not have any solutions. For example, consider the following augmented matrix:

Content:
[MATH: M = [1|− 2|3; 0|0|10]]

Content:
The corresponding system is
[MATH: x − 2y = 3; 0x + 0y = 10.]

Content:
The final equation, [MATH: 0x+0y=10,] has no solution. It simplifies to [MATH: 0=10,] which is a false statement.

Content:
So, there is no pair [MATH: x,y] that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

Item 6 — Example: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

Example Prompt:
Consider the system of linear equations
[MATH: 2x + 5y = 4; 4x + 10y = 0.]
Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

[MATH: 2|5|4; 4|10|0]

Reducing [MATH: M] to row echelon form, we have
[MATH: M|∼[2|5|4; 4|10|0]|R_{1}|:=(1)/(2)R_{1}; ∼[1|(5)/(2)|2; 4|10|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 4)R_{1}; ∼[1|(5)/(2)|2; 0|0|− 8].]

The corresponding system is now
[MATH: x + (5)/(2)y = 2; 0x + 0y = − 8.]

However, the final equation [MATH: 0x+0y=-8] has no solution. It simplifies to [MATH: 0=-8,] which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair [MATH: x,y] that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System

Content:
Given a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

Content:
- The system has exactly one solution if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called consistent independent.
- The system has infinitely many solutions if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only [MATH: 0]'s. These systems are called consistent dependent.
- The system has no solution if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only [MATH: 0]'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called inconsistent systems.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b0ff3e456c0e81795741fc6b263169da]

Content:
Note: A system of linear equations of the form
[MATH: ax + by = 0; cx + dy = 0,]
where we have only [MATH: 0]'s on the right-hand side, is called homogeneous. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: y=0.] Or, in vector form, [MATH: \langle 0,0 \rangle.]
